title: Deep rivers are quiet
hookLine: to Nalaka: shallow streams are noisy, the great river flows quietly

lines: HE TELLS HIS NEPHEW: GO TO HIM.
cards: Early on this path, you met an old sage named Asita. He held the newborn prince, smiled, and then wept, because he knew he wouldn't live long enough to hear this child teach.
The Sutta Nipata keeps that scene as the opening of a longer poem, and adds something you didn't hear then.
Before he died, Asita told his nephew, a young man named Nalaka: when you hear that this one has awakened, go to him. Nalaka waited. Years later, he went.

teach.h: THE WAY OF THE SAGE IS HARD.
teach.b: Nalaka asks about the life of a sage, what the Pali calls moneyya, the way of silence.
The Buddha warns him first that it's hard, then gives a long answer: be the same whether praised or insulted; go for alms without lingering, without wanting more; don't make a show of yourself.
Toward the end comes the image. Learn it, he says, from the water.
In the clefts and gullies, the little streams run noisily. The great waters move in silence. Then plainly: what is lacking makes a noise; what is full is quiet.
And one more picture: the fool is like a half-full pot, sloshing; the wise one is like a lake filled to the brim. A half-full water jug in the back of a car slaps and gurgles at every bump.
A full one makes no sound at all. The poem isn't saying never speak. The same answer praises a sage who speaks, when he does, about what is useful and true.
When the sage teaches, he teaches from what he knows, without excess. The noise comes from the gap, from the part that's empty and wants to be seen.
So the quiet isn't a rule of silence. It's what fullness sounds like.

how: Many Buddhist monasteries keep times of noble silence, and lay retreats often run for days with little or no talking, as a way of letting the mind settle.

o: a vow to never speak another word
a monk's alms, gathered in silence
the way of a sage: quiet fullness

games.q: deep rivers are quiet: tap the pairs.
p: the old sage who wept over the child
Asita's nephew, who waited and went

s: the Nalaka Sutta says a sage should never speak
it praises speech that is useful and true; the noise it warns about comes from what's lacking.
Asita sent his nephew to the Buddha
before he died he told Nalaka to go when he heard the child had awakened.
the Buddha told Nalaka the way of the sage was easy
he warned him first that it's hard to do.

games.q: you're Nalaka. your uncle, a great sage, told you long ago to seek out a child he blessed, once that child became awakened. you hear the news. what do you do?
o: go and ask him about the way of the sage.
games.why: he goes and asks about moneyya, the way of silence. the answer ends with the quiet river and the full lake.

practice: Picture a wide, slow river at evening: so much moving under the surface, and so little sound. Notice your own inner chatter, the little streams, without trying to stop it.
Let the breath go deeper and slower beneath it, like the river under the ripples, and rest down there.

wordCard.voice: Moneyya, the way of silence. The Buddha's image for Nalaka: little streams rush noisily, the great waters move in silence; what's empty makes noise, what's full is still.

orig.note: Pali moneyya: the way of a muni, a sage; tradition links muni, sage, with mona, silence. Nalaka asks about it in Sn 3.11.

carryVoice: Your line: what is full is quiet. A pause doesn't always need filling. Until tomorrow.

sources.ref: Sutta Nipata 3.11 (Nalaka Sutta), with its prologue on Asita
